record.experiment_description:
INTRODUCTION:
The Institute for Environmental Medicine together with the Environmental Biomedical Stress Data Center combine to form the nation's leading authority on the tolerance of living systems to adverse environments. The Institute for Environmental Medicine is the national center for the study of human oxygen tolerance and its extension. The fundamental research provides the basis for the development of hyperbaric oxygen therapy, and for the general use of oxygen in medicine. The Environmental Biomedical Stress Data Center is the international repository of technical data, information, and reports related to human existence in stressful environments in aerospace, under water, and Earth atmospheres.

BACKGROUND
The foundation for the Environmental Biomedical Stress Data Center was laid in 1965 when the U.S. Navy Surgeon General requested that the University of Pennsylvania devise safeguards for Naval and other undersea biomedical research data, that had in the past been scattered, often unavailable, or in some cases permanently lost. In parallel, the University of Pennsylvania expanded its environmental research facilities and established a national center for research, the Institute for Environmental Medicine (IFEM) (founded by Christian J. Lambertsen), to obtain new information concerning diving, manned aerospace activity, decompression, and effects of hyperbaric and hypobaric atmospheric exposures.

MODERN DAY DATA CENTER
The success of the original project at preserving, storing, and providing access to validated data made it sensible to extend the scope of function. This was accomplished by establishing the EBSDC in close relation with the IFEM. This extension of scope enabled collaborative retrieval, analysis, and modeling of physical and respiratory environment-relevant information concerning:

  • tolerance of human organs to oxygen poisoning
  • respiratory and pulmonary effects
  • physical work capability
  • narcotic influences and mental performance
  • speech capability
  • hydrostatic effects
  • thermal effects
  • decompression sickness and isobaric counter-diffusion gas lesion diseases
  • therapy of decompression sickness generated in extreme, working and shallow diving, and manned aerospace activity.

    The present data system plans involve continuing to provide a mechanism for acquiring new information and integrating it with data already obtained. This allows continuing development of new analytical methods for improvement in human capability, safety in environmental extremes, and applications to clinical therapy situations. Current research interests are:

  • acute and sustained adaptations to natural and synthetic respiratory environments at rest and at work
  • control of internal oxygen and acid-base environments
  • extension of tolerance to oxygen and hypoxia in clinical, atmospheric, undersea and aerospace circumstances
  • gas narcosis, density, and toxic effects
  • decompression and isobaric gas lesion diseases
  • measurement of limits of human physical, physiologic and cognitive performance in extreme environments
  • technology transfer through Environmental Biomedical Research Data Center.

    Summary of Research Program: Use of altered environmental gases, pressures and temperatures to magnify and make measurable changes in fundamental respiratory, neural and cardiovascular functions, to elucidate normal regulatory mechanisms, and to study their disruption by graded exposures to environmental extremes. Development of advanced decompression procedures. Human beings are used as appropriate for the effects and mechanisms examined. Chemical, electrical, flow, histopathology, neuromuscular functions and mental functions are employed to track isolated or concurrent effects of purposeful activity or external physical or chemical stress. Research emphasizes quantitative separation of effects of oxygen, pressure and inert gas components upon specific tissue and organ functions. Measurements of effect are followed by study of methods to prevent or extend tolerance to effects (e.g., hyperoxia, hypoxia, narcosis). Results are applicable to clinical use of oxygen and hyperbaric oxygen therapy, to manned undersea and aerospace activity, synthetic biologic fluids, anesthesia, and influences of drugs upon mental and physical functions.

    Research techniques include dynamic measurement of human respiratory reactivity, blood and brain acid-base and oxygenation states; mental, psychomotor and sensory performance measurement; retinal electrical activity and visual evoked potential; Doppler monitoring of vascular gas embolism; and predictive modeling of interactions of environmental stress effects on physiologic functions.

    ACCESS VIA THE WEB

    The Institute for Environmental Medicine and the Environmental Biomedical Stress Data Center both maintain public websites:

    Institute for Environmental Medicine. The Institute for Environmental Medicine website offers information on research and training programs along with descriptions of the core facilities of the Institute. This site also lists the current staff members and also gives profiles of the investigators currently doing research at the institute. A detailed description of the hyperbaric treatment program offered at the institute is also given.

    Environmental Biomedical Stress Data Center. The Environmental Biomedical Stress Data Center website offers access to the data center's extensive catalog of reports and technical publications, encompassing periods prior to current Medline or other computer searchable bibliographical systems. The data center also provides access to much of the past 50 years of diving decompression methods and concepts generated internationally by Naval, Industrial and University aegis. The predictive studies section of the website represents conjoined investigations by individual scientist, associated laboratories, and collaborating national agencies. A central purpose is to obtain concurrent measurements of multiple physiologic effects and recovery, in response to graded degrees and durations of imposed specific environmental stresses.

    Such functions provide a living and growing archive of hard data used as a basis for direct support of national and international agencies in design of new programs or research, and especially for the integration and quantitative predictive modeling of methods for describing human physiologic tolerance and performance capabilities. The predictive models are used as practical for application to development of new procedures, to improve safety and capability in adverse environmental situations. It has been the basis for continuing scientific advisory functions to NASA, Navy and other federal agencies, universities, and industry from its origins to the present.
